title: Practice Date

jokes.text: Councilman Dexhart's apology: 'I was making love to a beautiful woman... and her boyfriend, and a third person whose name I never learned.'
jokes.setup: A politician begins what sounds like a heartfelt apology to his wife for an affair
jokes.punchline: He reveals it was a four-way encounter — escalating absurdly from a simple affair
jokes.explanation: Strong cold open escalation: the apology format creates expectations, and each new detail is more absurd than the last. 'Third person whose name I never learned' is a well-timed specificity gag.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Dexhart
dialogue.line: I want to apologize to my wife, my constituents, and the good people of Pawnee for my infidelity. I made a terrible mistake.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Dexhart
dialogue.line: It started as a simple affair, but then it became a threesome. And then a foursome.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Dexhart
dialogue.line: I don't even know who the fourth person was.

jokes.text: 'Furthermore, it was wrong of me to say I was building houses for the underprivileged when I was actually having four-way sex in a cave in Brazil.'
jokes.setup: The politician continues his apology, doubling down on revelations
jokes.punchline: The cover story (building houses) is comically contrasted with the reality (cave sex in Brazil)
jokes.explanation: The escalation continues beautifully. 'Houses for the underprivileged' vs 'four-way sex in a cave in Brazil' is a perfect juxtaposition of noble cover story and outrageous reality.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Dexhart
dialogue.line: I was doing important charitable work in Brazil, building schools for underprivileged children.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's wonderful! What kind of schools?

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Dexhart
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I wasn't building schools. I was at a cave orgy.

jokes.text: 'I bet cave sex is in-sane.' / 'Why?' / 'The echoes and the humidity.'
jokes.setup: Someone has just reported on the cave sex scandal as if it's shocking and shameful
jokes.punchline: Tom responds with genuine enthusiasm and specific sensory logic for why cave sex would be great
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the cold open. Instead of being scandalized, Tom pivots to genuinely endorsing cave sex with specific, pseudo-scientific reasoning ('echoes and humidity'). The deadpan specificity is the craft — it's not just 'cave sex sounds fun,' it's a confident sensory argument. Perfect economy, total character integration (this is exactly Tom Haverford logic), and the setup/punchline structure is immaculate. Earns 8+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I mean, think about the acoustics. Everything echoes. It would be deafening.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And the moisture. Caves are damp. That's just unpleasant.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Plus, stalagmites. Very pointy.

jokes.text: Councilman Dexhart had sex with a prostitute in a limousine 'on the way to AND from the press conference where he apologized for having an affair.'
jokes.setup: Each revelation about Dexhart's scandal is more outrageous than the last
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'on the way to AND from' the apology press conference is the comedic kicker — he literally sandwiched the apology with prostitutes
jokes.explanation: The 'to AND from' detail is the key comedic move here — the symmetry of sandwiching an apology with the exact behavior you're apologizing for is excellent structural irony. Well-crafted escalation beat.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Dexhart
dialogue.line: I was going to say the cave was naturally occurring and I was simply exploring it for geological research.

jokes.text: 'Why does anybody want to run for public office? You're just asking to have your entire life exposed.' / 'Well, if you're squeaky clean, like I am, there's no problem.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks rhetorically why anyone would want to run for office given all this exposure
jokes.punchline: Ron (who hits on women constantly) declares himself squeaky clean with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Ron's self-delusion is well-deployed here. It's a setup for the punchline that immediately follows (the rebuttal about hitting on women), so it functions as the first half of a two-beat joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I don't care about the scandalous details. I'm focused on policy, not gossip.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: But did you know that he was seen at that restaurant with someone who wasn't his wife? And apparently they ordered the expensive wine! The EXPENSIVE wine!

jokes.text: 'You're married, and you hit on women constantly.' / 'Yeah, but I've never sealed the deal. Just window shopping.'
jokes.setup: Ron claims to be squeaky clean
jokes.punchline: He admits to constant hitting-on-women but reframes it as morally neutral 'window shopping'
jokes.explanation: 'Just window shopping' is a great line — it reframes marital infidelity-adjacent behavior with a breezy commercial metaphor. Very Ron Swanson in its confident self-justification. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: News Reporter
dialogue.line: Councilman Dexhart issued a statement today saying he had sex during the trip to apologize for having sex.

jokes.text: 'You can fly to Brazil, just don't enter the cave. Up top.'
jokes.setup: The 'window shopping' logic about not crossing the line
jokes.punchline: Applies the same logic to the Dexhart scandal — the cave being the metaphorical point of no return — and requests a high-five
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback that crystallizes the window-shopping metaphor by returning to cave sex. 'Don't enter the cave' as a metaphor for fidelity is economical and funny. 'Up top' punctuates it perfectly — he's proud of this wisdom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. I would never cheat on Aunty. I love that woman. Look, when you're in a committed relationship, you don't go to other stores. You shop at the same store. Sure, maybe you go to a different aisle to look at some things, maybe you pick up some items you weren't supposed to pick up, but at the end of the day, you check out at the same register.

jokes.text: The dirt-digging game setup: 'You will never believe what I just found on Jerry's Facebook.' / 'A friend.' / 'Burn.'
jokes.setup: Tom announces breathlessly that he found something on Jerry's Facebook
jokes.punchline: The 'dirt' is that Jerry has a friend — implying he's so pathetic this counts as shocking news
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical. 'A friend' is a two-word punchline that lands because of perfect misdirection — the breathless setup implies something scandalous, and 'a friend' reframes his singular friend as the scandal. The follow-up 'Burn' from April is perfectly dry. Good Jerry-as-office-punching-bag comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: It's like that time we found out about the cave sex scandal. We all knew we were crossing a line, but nobody wanted to be the first one to say it.

jokes.text: Jerry: 'Okay, again, I'd really rather not play.' (repeated protests throughout the scene)
jokes.setup: Everyone insists Jerry participate in the dirt-digging game despite his protests
jokes.punchline: His repeated, increasingly plaintive refusals are ignored by everyone
jokes.explanation: Classic Parks Jerry joke — he knows something bad will happen, protests reasonably, and is steamrolled. Character-specific and sets up later payoffs. Not a sharp one-liner but functional running gag infrastructure.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I'm squeaky clean. I have no scandals.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Really? Nothing?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Well, in high school I got detention for returning a library book three days late. And one time I jaywalked.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's it?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I also once wore a white shirt after Labor Day.

jokes.text: After Jerry learns about his public urination charges: 'He's probably gonna go anger pee in the courtyard.'
jokes.setup: Jerry is embarrassed and upset about his public urination record being exposed
jokes.punchline: A coworker speculates that his response to this humiliation will be... more public urination
jokes.explanation: 'Anger pee' is a great compound noun invention. The joke is both a callback and a character-defining absurdist extension — framing urination as a coping mechanism specific to Jerry. Tight and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, what did you find on Facebook?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry actually has a friend request from someone.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's... that's actually amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry having even one friend is noteworthy.

jokes.text: Dave and Leslie's awkward goodbye: 'Roger that.' / 'Copy. Over and out.'
jokes.setup: Dave says he'll see Leslie tomorrow for their first date and there's a normal goodbye moment
jokes.punchline: Leslie responds with walkie-talkie police jargon, completely undermining the romantic moment
jokes.explanation: Very Leslie Knope — her nervous energy comes out as hyper-competent procedural language in a romantic context. The escalation from 'Roger that' to the full 'Over and out' shows her doubling down on the awkwardness. Character-specific and charming.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Jerry's upset about the game. He'll probably go home, make a pot of coffee, and just... sit there drinking it until he feels better.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Or he'll reorganize his garage for the third time this week.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He's definitely going to eat an entire meatloaf by himself while watching home videos of his kids.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The man will consume a bottle of scotch and contemplate the futility of sports.

jokes.text: Leslie talking-head confessional: 'I'm not nervous. Why should I be nervous? We're just two people going on a first date. There's nothing to be nervous about.' — clearly extremely nervous.
jokes.setup: Leslie is about to go on a first date with Dave
jokes.punchline: Her repeated insistence that she's NOT nervous is the most nervous-sounding thing imaginable
jokes.explanation: The 'protesting too much' joke is a well-worn format but Leslie's specific cadence and energy make it work. The talking-head format suits this kind of unintentional self-revelation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: So we're still on for Friday night?

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Affirmative. 1900 hours. I will arrive at your location.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Why are you talking like that?

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: You said to be formal. I am implementing formal protocols.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I meant like, nice formal. Not military formal.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Understood. Changing communication frequency to civilian-standard protocol.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Thank you.

jokes.text: Someone is at the government office searching for dirt on co-workers. Outsider: 'My taxes pay your salary, right? Cool.'
jokes.setup: A government worker is openly conducting a personal game on work time when a taxpaying citizen walks by.
jokes.punchline: The citizen's response — 'My taxes pay your salary, right? Cool.' — is perfectly resigned civic disappointment delivered without anger.
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational joke about the absurdity of government work. The 'Cool' is the punchline — complete acceptance and resignation. Good economy but not especially character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm not nervous, I'm just... I have a lot of energy. I drank like four cups of coffee this morning, and I might have eaten an entire box of calzones. So if I seem a little flustered, it's just the calzones and the coffee, not because I'm going on a date with Ben tonight.

jokes.text: Leslie interrupts a story about someone's life being saved to ask Ann for first date outfit advice, specifically requesting 'a pair of cargo pants' and 'a sexy hat'.
jokes.setup: Ann is mid-story about an emotional life-saving moment
jokes.punchline: Leslie barges in asking about cargo pants and 'a sexy hat' for her date, completely derailing the moment
jokes.explanation: 'A sexy hat' is the linchpin — it's a genuinely weird fashion concept that reveals Leslie's cluelessness about dating while being specific enough to be funny. Ann's 'I don't know what that even is' reaction is the perfect straight-man beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I've been digging into some things at City Hall. Building records, permit applications, financial discrepancies.

dialogue.speaker: Justin Anderson
dialogue.line: Ron, that's... you know that's using government resources for personal investigations, right?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I'm doing it on my lunch break.

dialogue.speaker: Justin Anderson
dialogue.line: Your lunch break is three hours long.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I'm a slow eater.

jokes.text: Ann responds to 'a sexy hat': 'I don't know what that even is.' / Leslie: 'Helping already.'
jokes.setup: Leslie requests a 'sexy hat' as first date attire
jokes.punchline: Ann's genuine bafflement is immediately reframed by Leslie as positive progress
jokes.explanation: Leslie's 'Helping already' is delusionally optimistic spin on a total non-answer. Perfect Leslie character comedy — she finds encouragement in confusion. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What do you think? Cargo pants or... cargo pants?

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Leslie, those are the same thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: No, see, one has the extra pockets on the legs. That's the sexy one.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: That's not what 'sexy' means.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, I'm also wearing my sexy hat.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Which one is that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I haven't decided yet.

jokes.text: Tom holds up a photo: 'Taliban robes!' / Ron: 'What? Where'd you get that photo from?' / 'Those aren't taliban robes. That's from Halloween. I was dressed like a jedi.'
jokes.setup: Tom dramatically reveals what looks like a photo of Ron in Taliban robes
jokes.punchline: Ron's entirely plausible defense is that it was a Halloween Jedi costume — visually indistinguishable to voters
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: Ron in a Jedi robe being indistinguishable from Taliban dress is both absurdist and a sharp political observation about how optics work. 'I'm sure voters could tell the difference' dripping with sarcasm is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: I can help you later.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Later? Ann, I need help now. What if I die before later?

jokes.text: 'Did everybody know that Ron's ex-wife Tammy is actually his second ex-wife named Tammy? That's right. Ron has two ex-wives, each named Tammy.' / 'Both of them bitches.' / 'Yes, my mom's name is Tammy.'
jokes.setup: Someone reveals Ron has two ex-wives both named Tammy
jokes.punchline: Ron: 'Both of them bitches.' Then the kicker — 'Yes, my mom's name is Tammy.'
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode and one of the show's great character reveals. It's a three-beat escalation: (1) both ex-wives are named Tammy — absurd and funny on its own, (2) 'Both of them bitches' — Ron's brutal matter-of-fact delivery is perfect character comedy, (3) 'Yes, my mom's name is Tammy' — the devastating kicker that adds a Freudian psychological layer without over-explaining it. The structure is immaculate: each beat earns the next. It's deeply character-specific (this is pure Ron Swanson mythology), original, and highly quotable. Easily the best joke in the episode and earns 8+ on craft.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Look, this receipt is completely legitimate. I have documentation for everything.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown character
dialogue.line: Tom, this receipt is from a store that doesn't exist.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. But check out this photo instead.

jokes.text: 'Tom! That was a jaeger-secret. You just breached a jaeger-secret.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just revealed the two-Tammys secret publicly
jokes.punchline: Ron chastises him using his own invented portmanteau word 'jaeger-secret' (a secret so classified it's like a Jägermeister-level secret)
jokes.explanation: 'Jaeger-secret' is a Tomism — a made-up compound that sounds like Tom invented a classification system for secrets. Slightly unclear on exactly what a jaeger-secret is, which dilutes it, but the invented word is charming and character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I was not defending the Taliban. I was making a point about the geopolitical complexities of nation-building in Central Asia.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: But apparently, I have a naive faith in voters' ability to distinguish context.

jokes.text: Ann in a store with Leslie, trying on an outfit: 'Will you be wearing it out of the store today, madame?' / 'I think I will, good lady.'
jokes.setup: Ann is helping Leslie prepare for her date by finding an outfit
jokes.punchline: Ann plays along with the formal 'madame/good lady' register as if they're in a 19th century boutique
jokes.explanation: A light, pleasant character moment but not a strong joke. The playfulness is warm but not particularly original or specifically character-driven beyond 'two women having fun shopping.'

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I don't care.

jokes.text: Leslie's spiraling hypothetical fears: 'What if I get drunk and I talk about Darfur too much? Or not enough?'
jokes.setup: Ann tells Leslie to relax about the date
jokes.punchline: Leslie's list of hypothetical disasters reveals a very specific Leslie Knope-shaped anxiety — not whether to discuss Darfur, but getting the exact right amount
jokes.explanation: The Darfur line earns 8+ because it's such a precise character joke. It's not just 'Leslie talks about serious topics too much' — the addition of 'or not enough' shows her genuine moral anxiety about whether she's doing enough about world crises even on a first date. Only Leslie Knope would worry about under-discussing Darfur. High originality, excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I've been married three times. Three ex-wives. I have no idea what my mother's name is.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: What? Ron, that's your mother.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I know who she is. I just don't know her name. Could be Tammy. Could be Susan. All I know is she's a bitch, just like the other three.

jokes.text: Leslie reads from note cards: 'What if he shows up with another woman? What if one of my sleeves catches on fire and it spreads rapidly? What if, instead of tic tacs, I accidentally pop a couple of ambien and I have to keep punching my leg to stay awake?'
jokes.setup: Ann tries to assure Leslie that nothing will go wrong
jokes.punchline: Leslie's prepared note cards of disaster scenarios escalate from plausible to absurd ('sleeve catches fire') to specific-weird ('punching my leg to stay awake')
jokes.explanation: The note cards themselves are a visual gag (Leslie has literally prepared catastrophe scenarios in written form). The escalation from 'another woman' to 'sleeve fire' to 'Ambien leg-punching' is well-calibrated — each beat is more specific and absurd. The visual of Leslie solemnly reading these from cards is the comedic cherry on top.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Ron, I found your old diary from summer camp. It says here you cried during the final campfire song.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Haverford, you have committed a Category Five breach of the Swanson Code. I'm placing you under citizen's arrest for emotional espionage.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Those are all insane hypotheticals, and I promise you they won't happen.' / Leslie: 'They have happened. All of these have happened to me.'
jokes.setup: Ann dismisses Leslie's disaster scenarios as impossible
jokes.punchline: Leslie reveals they've all actually happened to her, retroactively making every absurd scenario plausible and tragic
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best structural jokes in the episode. Ann's dismissal sets up a classic misdirect — we expect Leslie to accept reassurance, but instead we learn the note cards weren't hypotheticals, they were a memoir. 'All of these have happened to me' recontextualizes everything and earns a big laugh. The economy is near-perfect ('They have happened' is four words that do enormous work).

dialogue.speaker: Store Employee
dialogue.line: Will that be all for you today?

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Yes, thank you so much.

dialogue.speaker: Store Employee
dialogue.line: Great. Will you be wearing that out of the store?

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Oh, um, yes, I suppose I will be.

dialogue.speaker: Store Employee
dialogue.line: Wonderful. That'll be $47.99.

jokes.text: Leslie's catalogue of actual dating disasters: vinegar mistaken for terrible wine, 3D glasses guy, sidecar detachment down stairs, man trying to pull her tooth while she slept — 'We went out after that, but then he got weird.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is listing the real disasters that have happened to her on dates
jokes.punchline: The tooth-pulling man is the darkest, most absurd entry — and then 'we went out after that, but then he got weird' reveals Leslie's absolutely broken threshold for what constitutes 'weird'
jokes.explanation: The cascade of absurd dating disasters is excellent, but the kicker is the real genius: Leslie continued dating a man who tried to pull her tooth while she slept, and HE got weird. This single line reveals volumes about Leslie's tenacious optimism and her total inability to properly evaluate red flags. It's deep character comedy and earns 8+ for the 'he got weird' capper specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: So are you married?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: No, but I'm working on it. I've created a whole backstory. His name is Dr. Richard Neville. He's a cardiac surgeon in Portland. We met at a medical conference. Well, I didn't actually go to the conference, but I've photoshopped myself into pictures from it.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: He has a boat. I've named it. The SS Knope-Neville. I've already planned our divorce. It's going to be very amicable. We'll spend summers together in the Hamptons.

jokes.text: Ann's additional bad date history: 'One time, I accidentally drank an entire bottle of vinegar. I thought it was terrible wine.' / 'Once, I went out with a guy who wore 3-D glasses the entire evening.' / 'One time, I rode in a sidecar on a guy's motorcycle, and the sidecar detached and went down a flight of stairs.'
jokes.setup: Ann starts listing her own past dating disasters.
jokes.punchline: Each disaster is more absurd and specific than the last — the vinegar wine mistake is human error, the 3D glasses is date weirdness, but the sidecar stairs is physically harrowing.
jokes.explanation: Great escalating list. The vinegar/wine mistake is the most relatable (being a bad wine judge), the 3D glasses date is the most unsettling (commitment to a bit), and the sidecar stairs is the most physically absurd. Good joke architecture.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What if he thinks I'm too enthusiastic? What if he finds out I have a folder labeled 'Future Ben Scenarios'? What if we go to dinner and the restaurant has those chairs that spin and I accidentally launch myself into the kitchen? What if I sneeze on him? What if I sneeze on him and it's a really wet sneeze? What if he thinks I'm a wet sneezer and tells all his friends and I become known throughout Pawnee as the Wet Sneezer?

jokes.text: Leslie anticipates the earpiece date-coaching plan, names it accurately before Ann can suggest it: 'I know what you're thinking. I wear an earpiece, you sit at a table nearby... let me tell you, it never works.'
jokes.setup: Ann is about to propose a solution to Leslie's date anxiety
jokes.punchline: Leslie has clearly tried the movie-style earpiece date plan before and it has a known failure rate
jokes.explanation: Subverts the rom-com trope by having Leslie pre-empt it and immediately dismiss it from experience. The fact that she knows 'it never works' from prior attempts is funnier than any earpiece plan could be. Good meta-rom-com awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Leslie, these scenarios are impossible. No one actually does these things.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ann, I've done all of them. Last week I got my arm stuck in a vending machine trying to retrieve a bag of chips that was hanging by a thread. The week before, I accidentally joined a cult. It was actually pretty well-organized.

jokes.text: Leslie's practice date note cards include: 'Whales, parades, electricity... and the rest are blank.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks what's on Leslie's topic note cards for practice conversation
jokes.punchline: She has three wildly unrelated topics and then nothing — the blank cards perfectly capture how Leslie's social anxiety has shut down her otherwise hyper-organized brain
jokes.explanation: The three topics are perfect: 'Whales, parades, electricity' — each one is something Leslie might genuinely be passionate about (she's a civic-minded Pawnee enthusiast), but as a date conversation list they're bizarre and unconnected. The blank cards are the kicker — this meticulous person gave up after three items. Earns 8+ for character specificity, economy, and the visual gag of the cards themselves.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: So there was this time I mistook vinegar for wine and drank the whole bottle.

jokes.text: Ann talking-head (or reaction): 'Leslie's in worse shape than I thought.' (watching Leslie practice laughing)
jokes.setup: Ann watches Leslie practice-laugh mechanically during their fake date
jokes.punchline: Ann's understated assessment paired with the clearly disturbing spectacle of Leslie's forced laugh
jokes.explanation: Functional deadpan reaction beat. Works in conjunction with the visual gag of Leslie's practice laugh (inferred from 'Is she practice laughing?' at 08:03). The camera cut to Ann is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: So I went on this date last week, right? And the guy shows up on a motorcycle with a sidecar. A SIDECAR. Who does that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Anyway, we're going down this hill, and the sidecar just detaches. It's rolling down the stairs, bouncing like a pinball, and I'm just sitting there screaming.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: The guy turns around and goes, 'Don't worry, that happens all the time.' ALL. THE. TIME.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm never dating again. I'm marrying Ben, adopting seventeen children, and we're moving to a compound.

jokes.text: 'Is she practice laughing?' (camera presumably cuts to Leslie doing a visible, mechanical fake laugh)
jokes.setup: Ann has set up a practice date scenario to help Leslie
jokes.punchline: Leslie is visibly practice-laughing in a way that is clearly horrifying to witness
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Leslie practice-laughing (presumably a mechanical, off-putting fake laugh) combined with Ann's horrified question is a strong moment. On rewatch, knowing what Leslie's practice laugh looks like makes this even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: They continued dating, but he got weird.

jokes.text: Leslie gives a 'thorough history of the teeter-totter' including the Danish word 'oppe og nede apparat' meaning 'the up and down machine'.
jokes.setup: The practice date has begun and Leslie needs to make conversation
jokes.punchline: She delivers a complete and apparently thorough academic history of the teeter-totter as date conversation
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Leslie — her anxiety manifests as hyper-prepared but completely inappropriate monologuing. The specific Danish terminology ('oppe og nede apparat') is a great detail showing she really researched this. 'The up and down machine' as a translation is also inherently funny. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: You should practice dating. Go on some practice dates.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Practice dates? That's like... like in a spy movie when they give you a fake identity and send you undercover, but then you get made and you have to escape the country.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: That's... not what practice dates are.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I know. I've already done it.

jokes.text: Ann asks Leslie to ask her a spontaneous question; Leslie freezes, then: 'How big is it?' / Ann: 'Really?'
jokes.setup: Ann tries to get Leslie to practice natural conversation by just asking 'the first thing that comes to you'
jokes.punchline: Leslie, freed from overthinking, immediately asks a sexually suggestive question ('How big is it?') — not intentionally, but revealing where her subconscious went
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it's plausibly innocent (she might mean 'how big is the department?' or 'how big is the cave?') but contextually reads as sexual. Ann's 'Really?' is perfectly calibrated. The character integration is strong — Leslie's subconscious mind going somewhere unexpected when unguarded is very true to her repressed enthusiasm.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I prepared some conversation topics for today.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Oh, that's nice. What did you come up with?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, I made it through three of them before I just gave up.

jokes.text: Tom confronts Donna: 'Donna, let me ask you something. Do you hate black people?' / 'Excuse me?' / 'Because apparently in 1988, you donated money to the presidential campaign for... David Duke!'
jokes.setup: Tom dramatically sets up what sounds like a serious accusation of racism
jokes.punchline: Donna's answer: 'I got a phone call. They said he would lower taxes.' — complete political naivety as a defense
jokes.explanation: Dark subversive joke that earns its edge. The punchline is Donna's utterly practical one-note defense: she was a single-issue voter who got cold-called. It satirizes both political naivety and the KKK guy's actual platform (tax cuts) without being preachy. The 'The KKK guy?' reaction beat amplifies it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ha ha ha! Oh that's funny! Ha ha!

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Leslie, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Practicing my laugh. I want to seem fun and carefree on my date.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: That's the least fun and carefree thing I've ever seen.

jokes.text: Donna: 'I got a phone call. They said he would lower taxes.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just revealed Donna donated to David Duke's presidential campaign
jokes.punchline: Donna's completely calm, practical explanation: a phone call promising lower taxes
jokes.explanation: This is a standalone 8 on economy alone. Nine words that do enormous satirical work: they simultaneously explain Donna's motivation (she's not racist, just easily swindled by tax-cut promises), satirize single-issue voting, and land with perfect deadpan delivery. The joke trusts the audience completely — no explanation needed. Just the flat, matter-of-fact line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: This is a seesaw. In Swedish, it's called a 'flicka-flicka.' No wait, that's not right. It's a 'se-saw-sen.' Actually, I think it might be 'flibbertigibbet.' You know what, I'm going to say it's definitely 'flibbertigibbet.'

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Leslie, those aren't real words.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: And this is a swing set, or as they call it in Germany, a 'schwing-schwang.' The French call it a 'le swing.' The Spanish call it... 'el swingo.' I'm very good at languages.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head: 'I've established a scientifically perfect ten-point scale of human beauty. Wendy is a 7.4, which is way too high for Tom, who is a 3.8. Ten is tennis legend Steffi Graf.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just shown off his wife Wendy to Ron
jokes.punchline: Tom has a 'scientific' beauty scale in which he ranks himself a 3.8 and his ideal is Steffi Graf specifically
jokes.explanation: This joke earns 8+ for three interlocking reasons: (1) Tom honestly assessing himself as a 3.8 is surprisingly self-aware for such an image-conscious character; (2) describing his own beauty scale as 'scientifically perfect' with decimal precision is peak Tom Haverford absurdist logic; (3) 'Ten is tennis legend Steffi Graf' is an inspired, specific, slightly left-field choice that defines the whole bit. Any number of celebrities could have been the '10' — Steffi Graf is specific enough to be funny on its own merits. High character integration, originality, and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: So Ann, I want to get to know you better. What's something that really gets you going?

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Oh! Um... I like gardening, I guess?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I mean, what really gets you... excited? What makes you... hot?

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Leslie, why are you asking me this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm trying to ask what your passions are! What do you like to... do... with your hands?

jokes.text: Ann opens the door to Leslie at night: 'You're late, and I can see your nipples through your dress.'
jokes.setup: Ann answers her door expecting Leslie for practice date night
jokes.punchline: Ann's greeting combines a normal critique (tardiness) with an extremely frank physical observation as if both are equally noteworthy
jokes.explanation: Ann's nurse-bluntness is well-deployed here. The structure of delivering both critiques in the same monotone register as if they're equivalent is the comedic technique. Good economy, good character integration (Ann's medical candor).

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Donna, I've been doing some research on your political donations.

dialogue.speaker: Donna Meagle
dialogue.line: Tom, you need to mind your business.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Well, I found something that's going to blow your mind. You donated $5,000 to the 'Friends of Sweetums' SuperPAC.

dialogue.speaker: Donna Meagle
dialogue.line: So?

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: So? Donna, that's a front group for Big Candy! You're on record as being against corporate sugar interests!

dialogue.speaker: Donna Meagle
dialogue.line: Tom, I didn't donate to Big Candy. I donated to my cousin Sweetums. He runs a frozen yogurt shop.

jokes.text: Ann as fake-Dave: 'You're 20 minutes late. I almost left.' / Leslie: 'I was... dropping my niece off.' / 'What's your niece's name?' / 'Torple. What? I don't know.' / 'That's not a name.' / 'I don't have a niece.'
jokes.setup: Ann is simulating a bad date to expose Leslie's anxious lying behavior
jokes.punchline: When pressed, Leslie invents a niece named 'Torple' — an obviously made-up name — then immediately confesses she has no niece
jokes.explanation: 'Torple' is the star of this joke — it's a genuinely brilliant random name that sounds like Leslie's panicked brain tried to generate a name and failed spectacularly. The rapid collapse from the lie ('Torple') to the realization ('What? I don't know') to the admission ('I don't have a niece') is perfectly paced cringe comedy. Earns 8+ for 'Torple' alone.

dialogue.speaker: Donna Meagle
dialogue.line: I didn't donate to the KKK. I donated to the KFC. Kentucky Fried Chicken. I got my letters mixed up, and honestly, the tax write-off was too good to pass up.

jokes.text: Leslie panics and excuses herself to the 'whizz palace... the place where you... you know, the toilet thing.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is floundering on the practice date and needs an escape
jokes.punchline: She calls the bathroom a 'whizz palace' and then cannot remember the actual word 'bathroom'
jokes.explanation: 'Whizz palace' is a funny coinage and pairs well with Ann's exasperated 'It's called a bathroom!' The joke is really about Leslie's social anxiety causing her to forget basic words. High character integration — only Leslie would euphamize a bathroom visit into something this grandiose and then completely blank on the actual word.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: My wife is an absolute goddess. Look at her. Just look at her. Those legs go all the way up.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy Haverford
dialogue.line: Tom, please stop.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: And her eyes? Her eyes are like two perfect spheres of beauty. I'm the luckiest man alive.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy Haverford
dialogue.line: This is so uncomfortable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Wait until you see her in a bikini. I'm serious, it's life-changing. I've seen grown men weep.

jokes.text: Ann snapping: 'It's a bathroom! It's called a bathroom!'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been spiraling and just called the bathroom a 'whizz palace'
jokes.punchline: Ann breaking her 'fake Dave' character to scream the word 'bathroom' is a great release beat
jokes.explanation: The punchline to the whizz palace setup. Ann's frustration breaking through her patient friend-coach persona is well-executed. Simple but effective escalation payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Tom's marriage is like a Steffi Graf rating system. It's perfect on paper, but nobody knows what the hell it means.

jokes.text: Ben (or coworker) vs. April: 'A little birdy told me you have one unpaid parking ticket.' / 'A little birdy told me your adoptive mother was arrested for marijuana possession.' / 'Snap!' / Beat. / 'I didn't know I was adopted.'
jokes.setup: Two people are trading mild dirt on each other; Jerry is watching
jokes.punchline: Jerry, who has just learned he was adopted via this petty game, delivers the devastating kicker with quiet devastation
jokes.explanation: This is the best-constructed joke in the episode and arguably in the show's early run. The structure is flawless: a seemingly petty exchange between two people about minor dirt (parking ticket vs. marijuana possession) accidentally detonates a nuclear bomb in Jerry's life. The beat of silence before 'I didn't know I was adopted' — perfectly placed — lets the horror land before the punchline. The show then piles on with immediate guilty sympathy. It's dark, escalating, structurally perfect, and it punishes Jerry (the series' running punching bag) in the most disproportionate way imaginable. Economy is near-perfect: seven words deliver an existential crisis. Strong 9+ on craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: You know what? Your hair looks like a dead animal.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's... that's perfect. That's exactly the kind of thing a bad date would say.

jokes.text: 'He totally baited you with that unpaid parking ticket.' (acknowledging the game's accidental cruelty)
jokes.setup: The aftermath of Jerry learning he was adopted
jokes.punchline: A coworker's analysis that reframes the adoption reveal as a tactical chess move rather than a life-altering tragedy
jokes.explanation: Good aftershock joke that extends the adoption beat. The framing of accidentally revealing someone's adoption as 'baiting' them demonstrates the show's commitment to keeping the game logic going even in disaster.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I was held up by a very important meeting with the city council.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Leslie, the city council meets on Tuesdays.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Right, yes, well this was an emergency meeting with Councilman... Blorgus McTimmerson.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Who?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Blorgus McTimmerson. He's very important and also very private.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Leslie, there is no Councilman McTimmerson.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. It was actually Councilman Blagnar Flibbertson. Completely different person.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: And he had a very important zoning issue about a... a haunted warehouse.

jokes.text: Tom's nickname game: 'Tom-mato sauce.' / Ron: 'Ron-tanamo bay.'
jokes.setup: Tom summons Ron to his office
jokes.punchline: They exchange elaborate name-puns ('Tom-mato sauce,' 'Ron-tanamo bay') as if this is a normal greeting ritual
jokes.explanation: 'Ron-tanamo bay' is the funnier of the two (the Guantanamo Bay reference applied to Ron's intimidating nature is an excellent pun). 'Tom-mato sauce' is weaker but serviceable. The joke is also in their casual mutual enjoyment of this wordplay — it suggests an ongoing bit between them that reveals unexpected warmth.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I need to excuse myself to the... the room where you go to... to do your business.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: You mean the bathroom?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Yes, but I can't say that word right now. I'm going to the... the porcelain throne chamber.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Leslie, just say bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I can't! I need to visit the... the number one and number two palace. Be right back.

jokes.text: Tom reveals to Ron that his marriage to Wendy is a green card sham: 'I just found out your wedding was a sham. It's a green card marriage.' / Ron: 'That's crazy. I was born in South Carolina. These colors don't run, baby.'
jokes.setup: Tom presents his winning dirt — that Ron's marriage is fraudulent
jokes.punchline: Ron misunderstands the accusation as being about his own patriotism/citizenship rather than his wife's
jokes.explanation: 'These colors don't run, baby' is pitch-perfect Ron Swanson — when accused of something, he responds with masculine American pride even when it's completely irrelevant. The misdirection works because it's so true to the character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, I got some dirt on you, Jerry. I found out you're adopted.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What? How did you... I didn't even know that!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, your parents never told you?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: No! I just found out through a board game!

jokes.text: Tom explains: 'We met in college. She wanted to work in the states. She couldn't get a permit.' / Tom: 'I knew it. I knew you couldn't get a wife as hot as her.'
jokes.setup: Ron explains the practical origin of his green card marriage
jokes.punchline: Tom's response reveals his actual subtext all along — he was never suspicious of wrongdoing, he just couldn't believe Ron landed a 7.4
jokes.explanation: Great callback to the beauty scale — Tom's investigation was always motivated by jealousy, not ethics. 'I knew you couldn't get a wife as hot as her' is brutally honest self-revelation from Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: You fake-married a Canadian woman to avoid taxes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. First of all, this is America. We don't question people's marriages here. That's what the Canadians do.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Tom, she IS Canadian.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Exactly! That's why I married her. To teach her about freedom.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Just admit that when it comes to digging up dirt, I bested you in this game. Say it. Say 'I bested you.'' / Ron: 'Fine, you bested me. Is that all?' / Tom: 'I'll have your wife tonight.' / Beat. / 'I'm just kidding. Get out of here.' / Ron: 'Why would you say that?'
jokes.setup: Tom has just won the dirt-digging game and made Ron say 'I bested you'
jokes.punchline: Tom escalates to 'I'll have your wife tonight' — which is both a power play and a terrible joke — then immediately walks it back, but Ron's genuine confusion ('Why would you say that?') is the real kicker
jokes.explanation: Tom's escalation from minor victory to making a pass at Ron's wife (even as a 'joke') is peak Tom Haverford overreach. Ron's 'Why would you say that?' is the character-specific reaction — he's not angry, just genuinely puzzled by this human behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I'd like to make a comment about Tom's wife, but I'm going to stop myself right there.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: You're welcome.

jokes.text: Ann (still fake-Dave) takes a phone call mid-date: 'I can't really talk right now, 'cause I'm on a date with this drip.'
jokes.setup: Ann is playing a terrible date to help Leslie build resilience
jokes.punchline: She refers to Leslie ('Dave's date') as 'this drip' during an actual phone call mid-date — the exposure therapy is extremely harsh
jokes.explanation: Ann committing to the awful-date bit by calling Leslie a 'drip' to a third party on the phone is a good escalation of the exposure therapy scenario. Shows Ann's commitment and the absurdity of the practice date premise.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: So I was thinking... maybe we could go back to your place and you could show me your... government files?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ann, no.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Too forward?

jokes.text: 'Do you want to watch a porno after this with me and my wife?' / 'No, Dave, 'cause you're disgusting.' / 'So it's definitely a no?'
jokes.setup: Ann is playing an increasingly terrible date to toughen Leslie up
jokes.punchline: She asks Leslie to watch pornography with her and her wife — and then checks if it's a 'definite' no, as if there's negotiating room
jokes.explanation: The callback 'So it's definitely a no?' is the best part — it transforms a shocking request into a negotiation, implying this is normal. Good economy and structure. The follow-up line about this being what dating is 'supposed to be' recontextualizes Ann's sadism as therapeutic.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Oh my god, Leslie, you actually stood up! That's amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I know, right? I've been practicing.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Well, it shows. I'm really proud of you.

jokes.text: Leslie breaks character: 'Why are you being so terrible? We're 2 people trying to go on a date. It's supposed to be fun. It's a date.' / Ann: 'You're right, it is.' / 'Well done.'
jokes.setup: Ann has been playing an increasingly awful date; Leslie pushes back
jokes.punchline: Ann immediately reveals this was the goal — getting Leslie to assert herself — and compliments her for it
jokes.explanation: The therapeutic misdirect — the horrible date was actually a test Leslie passed — is a warm comedic beat that works because we've been watching Leslie suffer. The sudden 'Well done' is a satisfying release.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Come on, Justin. I need dirt on Ron. Anything. A skeleton in his closet?

dialogue.speaker: Justin Anderson
dialogue.line: Well, there is one thing. Ron has a secret identity. He goes by the name Duke Silver.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Duke Silver? What is that?

dialogue.speaker: Justin Anderson
dialogue.line: I don't know exactly. But it's something he keeps very private. Very, very private.

jokes.text: 'You coy bastard.' (Leslie's apparently affectionate response to something)
jokes.setup: The practice date has just concluded positively
jokes.punchline: Leslie's affectionate 'You coy bastard' is a hilariously inappropriate term of endearment that reveals her fondness for Ann
jokes.explanation: Three words that characterize Leslie's unfiltered affection. 'Coy bastard' as an endearment is Leslie-specific — it's warm and strange at the same time. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I'm going to dig up dirt on you. I'm going to find out things about you that even you don't know.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Actually, that metaphor didn't really work.

jokes.text: 'There is a man named Duke Silver. He hangs out at a bar in Eagleton. He's an old friend of Ron's. Maybe you should ask him.'
jokes.setup: Someone is helping Tom find dirt on Ron; they offer a cryptic lead about a mysterious alter ego
jokes.punchline: The setup of 'Duke Silver' — a mysterious alter ego of Ron's — is a great tease that pays off in the jazz club scene
jokes.explanation: The Duke Silver setup is excellent comedy infrastructure — the straight-faced delivery of 'there is a man named Duke Silver' suggests this is a very serious secret. High rewatch bonus because knowing what Duke Silver is (a smooth jazz alter ego) makes the delivery even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Me power!

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: It's girl power, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I know what I said.

jokes.text: Tom's victory speech: 'I'm gonna dig up so much dirt, there's gonna be worms all over the place.' / Beat. / 'It sounded snappier in my head.'
jokes.setup: Tom is hyped up about finding dirt on Ron via the Duke Silver lead
jokes.punchline: He delivers a triumphant metaphor that immediately falls apart, then honestly admits it didn't land
jokes.explanation: This is a gem. The meta-commentary 'It sounded snappier in my head' is Tom Haverford at his finest — he knows he's a stylist who values cool-sounding lines, and he's self-aware enough to admit when one failed. The honesty of the assessment makes it funnier than the original line. Perfect economy. The beat before the self-correction is crucial.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Dave! Dave, open up! I'm here to tell you exactly what I think of you!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: AHHHHHHHHHHH! HELP! SOMEBODY HELP ME!

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head: 'Ann is so awesome. I'm lucky to have a friend who would spend a whole day being so mean to me.'
jokes.setup: Leslie reflecting on Ann's brutal exposure therapy practice date
jokes.punchline: She frames a day of being called a 'drip' and asked to watch pornography as a gift, because Leslie genuinely means it
jokes.explanation: Leslie's grateful sincerity makes this work — she genuinely thinks spending a day being insulted is a sign of friendship. High character integration: this optimistic interpretation of cruelty is pure Leslie Knope.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I am a GODDESS of municipal planning! I will reorganize this entire town by morning!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm going to rename all the streets after breakfast foods. Pancake Avenue. Waffle Lane.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: And it's going to be AMAZING because breakfast is the most important meal of the day, so obviously the streets named after it will be the most important streets.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm a genius. Has anyone told me I'm a genius tonight? Because I am.

jokes.text: Ann throws dress to Leslie: 'Catch.' / Leslie: 'I don't need your dress. I'm gonna wear my own stuff. Me power.'
jokes.setup: Ann is still trying to help Leslie with her outfit
jokes.punchline: 'Me power' — Leslie's triumphant, slightly unhinged declaration of confidence is delightfully odd
jokes.explanation: 'Me power' as a rally cry is a very specific Leslie Knope-ism. It's grammatically wrong in an endearing way and feels like something she genuinely says. Economy is perfect — two words, huge character.

dialogue.speaker: Club announcer
dialogue.line: Ladies and gentlemen, please welcome to the stage... the man, the myth, the legend... Duke Silver!

jokes.text: Ann's pep talk escalates to both women yelling 'Hell yeah! I am awesome! You are too!' repeatedly and increasingly loudly.
jokes.setup: Ann gives Leslie a genuine confidence-boosting speech before her date
jokes.punchline: The speech escalates into a mutual hype session where both women are screaming affirmations at each other
jokes.explanation: Warm and charming but not the sharpest comedy writing — this is more an emotional beat than a precision joke. The escalating affirmations are funny because of the performance energy, not because of any specific line or structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I'm Duke Silver.

dialogue.speaker: Duke Silver
dialogue.line: Hello, beautiful. I'm Duke Silver, and I'm here to play you some smooth jazz on my saxophone.

jokes.text: Leslie shows up at Dave's door drunk at midnight to announce she is 'awesome' and their date will be 'off the charts.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been hyped up by Ann and has drunk too much liquid courage
jokes.punchline: She arrives at a cop's door drunk at nearly midnight to deliver an unsolicited confidence speech
jokes.explanation: Leslie showing up drunk at a cop's house to declare her awesomeness is a perfect comedic character action — it's completely in character (she would do this) and demonstrates that all the practice date work has resulted in a different kind of disaster. The contrast between Ann's therapy and this outcome is great structural comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, is my shirt fused to my pants?

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Yeah, looks like it.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I don't know. I do know. I'm coming inside, so move. Okay? You make a better door than a guy.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is at Dave's door drunk and he's uncertain whether to let her in
jokes.punchline: 'You make a better door than a guy' — a scrambled/drunk version of 'you make a better door than a window,' delivered with confidence
jokes.explanation: The drunk mangled idiom is a great character beat — Leslie knows phrases exist but scrambles them ('better door than a guy' instead of 'better door than a window'). The confidence with which she delivers the scrambled idiom is the joke. High character integration — only Leslie would try to use an idiom while drunk and almost get it right.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Wait, did you just say 'lift'? Oh my God, yes! I would love a lift!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Blimey! Cheerio! Fish and chips! I'm speaking British now!

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I meant would you like me to give you a ride home.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: A ride? That's American. I'm committed to this bit.

jokes.text: Tom arrives at the bar asking for Duke Silver; the bartender says 'Yeah, he goes on in a second' — completely casual, as if it's normal.
jokes.setup: Tom has been given a cryptic lead about the mysterious 'Duke Silver'
jokes.punchline: The bartender treats 'Duke Silver' as completely ordinary — he's a regular performer here
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the Duke Silver mystery begins here. The bartender's casual 'yeah, he goes on in a second' is the first comedic beat — this intensely private, intimidating man has apparently been moonlighting as a jazz musician at a bar for years. High rewatch bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I cheated on a test in third grade. I looked over at Tommy's paper during the spelling bee.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I once told my mother her meatloaf was delicious when it was actually dry and terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I've been embezzling municipal funds for the past seven years and I've also been working with a Russian crime syndicate to smuggle counterfeit goods through the Parks Department.

jokes.text: Ron Swanson emerges as 'Duke Silver' — a smooth jazz saxophonist with a silky persona completely opposite to his Ron Swanson identity.
jokes.setup: The entire episode has established Ron as a hyper-masculine, private, no-nonsense authority figure
jokes.punchline: Ron has a secret alter ego as a smooth jazz musician who addresses the audience with lines like 'let the Duke Silver Trio take you on a little journey... to yourself'
jokes.explanation: Duke Silver is one of the greatest running character reveals in the show's history and this is its debut. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) The complete tonal inversion — Ron Swanson, aggressive libertarian meat-lover, is secretly a sensual jazz performer who says things like 'a little journey to yourself'; (2) The character integration is perfect — it reveals Ron has HIDDEN depths, not contradictory ones; he's passionate about music in the same way he's passionate about woodworking; (3) The specific language of 'Duke Silver' — the self-referential third person, the silky phrasing — is the best possible version of this joke; (4) Tom's witnessing it is the perfect comedic audience surrogate. This is a 9+ craft moment: the setup spans the whole episode, the reveal is earned, and the payoff recontextualizes Ron Swanson permanently.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: I once shot a man in Reno just to watch him die.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: No wait, that's a Johnny Cash song.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: But I did shoot someone for texting me after midnight. So you're welcome.

jokes.text: Duke Silver: 'both my albums are for sale here... Smooth as Silver and Hi Ho, Duke.' / 'And look for my new CD next month, Memories of Now.'
jokes.setup: Duke Silver has just finished his set
jokes.punchline: He has THREE albums, with titles that are parodies of smooth jazz album names — 'Smooth as Silver,' 'Hi Ho, Duke,' and 'Memories of Now'
jokes.explanation: 'Memories of Now' is inspired — it's the ideal parody of a pretentious smooth jazz album title, being simultaneously vague, philosophical, and meaningless. 'Hi Ho, Duke' and 'Smooth as Silver' are equally well-crafted jazz title parodies. Three albums' worth of commitment to the bit shows this is an actual double life. The accumulation of album titles escalates beautifully. 'Memories of Now' alone would earn this an 8.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Thank you. You've been a wonderful audience. I'm Duke Silver, and I'll be here all week.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: My latest album is called 'Smooth as Whiskey' — because that's what I am.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: My previous work includes 'Saxophonicity,' 'Duke Silver's Gone Fishin',' and my personal favorite, 'It's Called Woodworking and Also Music.'

jokes.text: Leslie's response to Dave's midnight confession: 'Is there anything you would like to share from your past to sort of balance the scales?' / 'One time, this guy rang my doorbell at midnight to brag about getting laid when he was 16, so I shot him. Good night.'
jokes.setup: After Dave's heartfelt midnight confession, Leslie is asked to reciprocate.
jokes.punchline: She recounts the exact scenario she's in as if it were a past event, ending with 'so I shot him' — delivered deadpan before 'Good night.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The structure is nearly perfect: Leslie recounts the exact current situation in past tense, which confirms she understands what's happening and is furious, then the escalation to 'I shot him' is unexpected and delivered as casual historical fact. The 'Good night' as a door-close button is impeccable timing. This is Leslie at her funniest — controlled, withering, and completely weird.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Ron, I got you. I got the photo. Duke Silver is real, and I have proof.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Tom, you've made a terrible mistake.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: No, I don't think I have. This is the greatest moment of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: That photograph means nothing. Duke Silver is a phantom. A ghost in the night.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Ron, come on. Just admit it. You're Duke Silver. You lost.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I admit nothing.

jokes.text: Ron, post-performance, negotiates with Tom: 'I have worked pretty hard to cultivate a certain authoritative or intimidating image around the office.' / Tom: 'Can I get a picture?' / 'Sure.' / 'Say, 'I bested you.'' / 'I bested you.'
jokes.setup: Ron is trying to keep Duke Silver secret from the office
jokes.punchline: Tom leverages his knowledge not for professional gain but to get Ron to say 'I bested you' on camera — connecting back to the dirt-digging game
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural callback — the episode's dirt-digging game concludes not with reporting anyone but with Tom extracting maximum personal satisfaction: a photograph of Ron (as Duke Silver) saying 'I bested you.' The tripling of this phrase through the episode gives it escalating comedic weight. Ron's willingness to comply shows his commitment to protecting Duke Silver.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Dave, I'm so sorry about last night. I think we should just cancel.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Cancel? Leslie, that was the best first date I've ever been on.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Really? I fell into the fountain, I tripped over my own feet, and I accidentally insulted your mother.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Exactly. You were genuine. You were real. Most first dates are so boring and fake. You just... you were you.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Thanks for lovin' the Duke.' / Tom: 'Lovely photo.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just gotten his photo with Duke Silver
jokes.punchline: Ron briefly slips back into Duke Silver mode ('Thanks for lovin' the Duke') before returning to Ron Swanson mode; Tom's prim 'Lovely photo' is a hilariously British-sounding satisfaction
jokes.explanation: 'Thanks for lovin' the Duke' in Ron's normal voice is a perfect character-split moment. 'Lovely photo' from Tom is unexpectedly formal and prim, which is funny coming from Tom Haverford. Both lines are quotable and earn this a solid 8.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I mean, he came to my house drunk, we didn't really talk about anything meaningful, and I'm pretty sure he threw up in my bushes. But you know what? That's good old-fashioned dating right there.

jokes.text: Ann tells someone she showed up drunk at Dave's house and didn't sleep with him. Response: 'You didn't sleep with him?' / 'Should I have?' / 'It never hurts.'
jokes.setup: Ann/Leslie recounts the embarrassing drunk house visit
jokes.punchline: The responder's matter-of-fact 'it never hurts' treats sleeping with a man while blackout drunk as the obvious tactically correct move
jokes.explanation: 'It never hurts' delivered with perfect blankness is good deadpan. The logic is sound in a completely wrong way. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: What? No one dug up anything on me? I'm disappointed. I have a documented scandal!

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: In 2006, I karate-kicked a door off its hinges at the community center.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: There's a full incident report. It's filed under 'Dwyer, Andy - Property Damage.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: I also got a noise complaint in 2009 for playing 'Bye Bye Bye' by *NSYNC* too loudly at 3 AM. The cops came!

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: And in 2011, I was banned from the Pawnee Public Library for trying to check out 47 DVDs at once.

jokes.text: Dave: 'You left quite a bit of stuff at my place last night... purse and earrings and a shoe.'
jokes.setup: The next morning, Dave reaccounts what happened when Leslie showed up drunk
jokes.punchline: The casualness of listing the items — 'purse and earrings and a shoe' (singular) — implies the level of chaos she caused
jokes.explanation: 'A shoe' (singular) is the tell-tale detail. Losing one shoe implies the kind of specific chaos that's harder to explain than losing both shoes. Dave's completely neutral recitation of the list is perfect deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: I wasn't getting plastic surgery. I got hit by an ambulance.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Dude, that's the luckiest thing I've ever heard.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'On my list of embarrassing things that I've done in my life, that was... numbers one through seven.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is apologizing for showing up drunk at Dave's house
jokes.punchline: She doesn't say 'it was the most embarrassing thing' — she says it occupied the TOP SEVEN slots, implying she has a ranked list of embarrassments this has displaced
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The specificity of 'numbers one through seven' is genius — it implies: (1) Leslie keeps an ongoing ranked list of her embarrassments; (2) this incident is so bad it didn't just top the list, it occupied seven consecutive slots; (3) there's still a list starting at #8 of other horrible things she's done. It's deeply character-specific (only Leslie would conceptualize her embarrassments as a ranked catalogue), economical, and highly quotable. Earns 8+ strongly.

jokes.text: Dave: 'You can make it up to me tonight on our second date.' / Leslie: '2nd?' / 'Last night was our first date, so that would make tonight our second.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is mortified and assumes Dave will cancel the date
jokes.punchline: Dave reframes her drunken midnight house visit as their 'first date' — rendering her whole elaborate preparation and practice date unnecessary, and saving her from embarrassment
jokes.explanation: Structurally satisfying episode callback — all of Leslie's preparation was for a first date that ended up happening drunk and uninvited. Dave being sweet about it by reframing it as 'the first date' is both comedically and emotionally satisfying. The joke is also in the irony: her worst possible version of a first date is still acceptable to Dave.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head: 'Well, we went on our first date, and I didn't even know it — a.k.a. I nailed it. No fires, no ambulances. Just good old-fashioned showing up drunk at a guy's house late at night.'
jokes.setup: Leslie reflects on how the first date went
jokes.punchline: She reframes 'showing up drunk at midnight' as 'good old-fashioned' courtship and considers this a win because there were no fires or ambulances
jokes.explanation: Excellent episode-concluding character joke. 'No fires, no ambulances' is a direct callback to Leslie's note-card disaster list — by her own metric of success (sleeves not catching fire, no ambulances), this was objectively a triumph. The reframing of drunk midnight showing-up as 'good old-fashioned' is deeply Leslie Knope. This earns 8+ for how fully it integrates character, callback, and irony in very few words.

jokes.text: Councilman Dexhart's final press conference clip: 'However, I want to be clear. I have no plans to resign.'
jokes.setup: The episode has used Dexhart's scandal as a recurring backdrop throughout
jokes.punchline: After all the revelations (four-way cave sex, cocaine, prostitutes en route to apology press conference), Dexhart's position is simply: no resignation
jokes.explanation: Good closure on the Dexhart running gag. The complete separation between the magnitude of the scandal and the lack of consequences ('no plans to resign') is sharp political satire. Economy is good — his statement is the entire joke.

jokes.text: Jerry's talking-head: 'Is it weird that my feelings are hurt that no one's found any dirt on me yet?'
jokes.setup: The dirt-digging game has resulted in multiple scandals for everyone — except Jerry (who had only public urination charges)
jokes.punchline: Jerry is hurt not by the game exposing him, but by being so boring that no one found anything else on him
jokes.explanation: A brilliant meta-Jerry joke. The running gag about Jerry is that bad things happen to him — but this subverts it by showing Jerry's fragile ego is actually hurt by NOT being interesting enough to have dirt. He'd rather be scandalous than boring. It's a deep character revelation played for comedy. High character integration and originality for a Jerry bit.

jokes.text: Another coworker reveal: 'Jerry, plastic surgery?' / Jerry: 'I got hit by a fire engine.' / 'You are so lucky.' / 'How?'
jokes.setup: Someone finds what looks like plastic surgery on Jerry's record
jokes.punchline: It's not plastic surgery — he got hit by a fire engine. Someone considers him 'lucky' for this. Jerry's 'How?' is the perfect devastated kicker.
jokes.explanation: The closing joke of the episode nails the Jerry formula with maximum efficiency. Four-beat structure: (1) suspicious finding; (2) devastatingly mundane/terrible explanation; (3) inexplicably positive spin from a coworker; (4) Jerry's quiet, confused 'How?' The 'lucky' reframe is the genius move — finding someone lucky for having been struck by an emergency vehicle requires such a specific kind of oblivious cheerfulness. 'How?' is one of the episode's most quotable single words. Excellent economy and character integration.

tmdb_overview: Leslie is nervous about her first date with Dave, so Ann takes her on a practice date to help her prepare. Meanwhile, after a local councilman is caught up in a sex scandal, Tom, Ron, April and Mark decide to see who can uncover the worst dirt on each other.
insight: Character comedy drives an 83-point episode through escalating absurdist setups rather than individual punchline moments.
